title: Circle the stronger nucleophile
asks: Two species are shown. Circle the one that attacks carbon faster in an {{SN2}} reaction.

know.h: Nucleophilicity is a rate: how fast a species displaces a leaving group in an {{SN2}} reaction. Basicity is an equilibrium ({{pKa}} of the conjugate acid). They often agree, but not always.
The lecture's sketch: basicity increases to the left and up in the periodic table; nucleophilicity increases to the left and down.
Across a row, nucleophilicity follows basicity: it increases to the left ({{H2N-}} > {{HO-}} > {{F-}}; {{NH3}} 8,000 against {{H2O}} 1).
Down a column, nucleophilicity increases while basicity decreases ({{I-}} > {{Br-}} > {{Cl-}} > {{F-}}; {{HS-}} > {{HO-}}): larger atoms are more polarizable and less tightly solvated.
Charge: an anion is a better nucleophile than its own neutral conjugate acid ({{HO-}} 16,000 against {{H2O}} 1). This rule compares the same atom only: neutral {{NH3}} (8,000) beats {{Cl-}} (1,000).
Bulk: with the same attacking atom, the bulkier species is the poorer nucleophile. tert-Butoxide, {{(CH3)3CO-}}, is a strong base but a poor nucleophile.
Resonance: a charge spread over several atoms is less available. Acetate (630) is far weaker than hydroxide (16,000), although both attack with a negative oxygen.
Know the {{pKa}} values that tempt you, so that you can recognize the stronger base and not be fooled by it: HI -10, HCl -8, {{H2S}} 10, {{H2O}} 15.7, {{CH3OH}} 15.5, {{(CH3)3COH}} 17.

Skill: find the atom that attacks (the one with the lone pair or the charge), and be able to say whether two atoms share a row or a column of the periodic table: C, N, O, F in one row; O above S; F, Cl, Br, I in one column.
Skill: draw the second resonance form of an anion (acetate, phenoxide, azide, tosylate) to see whether its charge is shared.

method: Find the atom that attacks in each species.
Same atom? The one with the negative charge wins; if both are charged, the less bulky and less delocalized one wins.
Different atoms in the same row? The one further left (the stronger base) wins.
Different atoms in the same column? The lower one wins, although it is the weaker base.
Neither the same row nor the same column, or two rules that disagree? Use the lecture table.
Check your answer against the lecture table whenever both species, or close relatives of them, are on it.

pitfalls.h: Choosing the stronger base when the atoms are in the same column (choosing {{Cl-}} over {{I-}}, or {{HO-}} over {{HS-}}).
Choosing tert-butoxide because it is the stronger base: bulk makes it the weaker nucleophile.
Circling a species only because it has a negative charge. The charge rule compares the same atom: {{NH3}} (8,000) beats {{Cl-}} (1,000) and {{CH3CO2-}} (630).
Missing resonance: acetate, phenoxide and tosylate have a negative oxygen, but the charge is shared, so they are weaker than hydroxide or an alkoxide.
